old: This project studies the design and implementation of a Caro web application together with a set of adversarial-search experiments and teaching materials. The report specifies a 15 × 15 Freestyle game, the board and move-history contracts, and the algorithms used to select and evaluate moves. It explains random and rule-based baselines, contiguous-run heuristics, tactical checks, Chebyshev candidate generation, soft candidate caps, Minimax and Alpha-Beta. It also treats iterative deepening, Zobrist hashing, transposition-table bounds, quiescence and incremental pattern counting in their corresponding reference or legacy implementations. Each algorithm is presented with its inputs, state, decision procedure, invariants, complexity, worked examples and limitations.
new: This project develops a web application for Caro on a 15 × 15 board under Freestyle rules and uses the game to study adversarial search. The application combines a React interface, a PixiJS board and a Rust engine compiled to WebAssembly, with search executed in a Web Worker. The report explains board representation, legal moves, win detection, heuristic evaluation, candidate selection, Minimax and Alpha-Beta pruning. It also examines hashing, transposition tables, quiescence and iterative deepening in separate reference and legacy implementations. The recorded native engine experiment contains 816 search measurements, including 408 paired Minimax and Alpha-Beta comparisons and 820 state-restoration checks. Separate records examine agreement between the JavaScript adapter and the WebAssembly binary, browser Worker responses and selected interface interactions. The reference experiments show that fewer visited nodes can coincide with longer execution time when move ranking adds work. They also identify immediate tactics lost by a hard candidate cap and an incorrect score caused by reusing cached entries after the root player changes. These results connect search algorithms to an interactive application and show why candidate policy, state restoration and cache context must be specified alongside search depth.

The report therefore studies move quality together with the controller checks that determine whether an AI response can be committed.

A heuristic gives a bounded estimate for nonterminal positions, while terminal outcomes take precedence. Minimax specifies alternating decisions; Alpha-Beta can discard branches that cannot alter the selected-tree value. Candidate generation restricts the search space, and ordering changes traversal order. The reference experiments further evaluate incremental Zobrist hashing, transposition-table bounds, and iterative-deepening budgets on controlled native benchmarks. Minimax defines alternating decisions, and Alpha-Beta pruning preserves the value of the same selected search tree while omitting branches that cannot change it. Candidate filtering changes the tree itself; ordering changes the sequence in which its moves are examined. The reference experiments extend this analysis to Zobrist hashing, transposition-table bounds and interrupted iterative search. [44] [8]
